To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a viscous blast-wave description of relativistic heavy ion collisions at the LHC is consistent with the data on transverse momentum spectra and anisotropic flows of identified particles for all centralities, and that the shear viscosity to the entropy density ratio $\simeq0.24$ is consistent with the results from the LHC.

a viscous blast-wave description of relativistic heavy ion collisions is able to describe the transverse momentum distributions and the flow harmonics for identified particles at the LHC, and that the extracted $\eta/s$ value is consistent with other recent estimates.

the blast-wave model with a viscosity-based survival time of geometrical perturbatives formed in the early stage of heavy-ion collisions can describe the transverse momentum distributions of identified particles as well as flow harmonics at the LHC with a shear viscosity to entropy ratio $\eta/s\sim 0.24$.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the viscous blast-wave modeling of relativistic heavy ion collisions and the estimation of shear viscosity to entropy ratio from the measured particle yields and flow coefficients.
the development of a model to study the transverse momentum distributions of particle yields and elliptic and triangular flows in heavy-ion collisions.
the development of a hydrodynamic model that can simultaneously describe the transverse momentum spectrum and the anisotropic flow of identified particles in the LHC data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study provides a new perspective on the role of viscosity in relativistic heavy-ion collision phenomenology.
the present study is a step forward in understanding the role of viscosity and its impact on the hydrodynamic evolution of heavy-ion collisions.
the LHC data on identified particle spectra and flow harmonics are well reproduced by a viscous blast-wave hydrodynamical model with $\eta/s\sim 1/4$.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the viscous blast-wave approach, which includes the effect of viscosity in the hydrodynamic evolution, provides a good description of the experimental data on particle production and flow harmonics for various centralities at the LHC.

the transverse momentum dependence of elliptic and higher harmonic flow harmonics can provide a useful constraint on the shear viscosity to the entropy density ratio of the quark-gluon plasma created in relativistic heavy-ion collision experiments at the LHC and the future Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) experiments.
a hydrodynamically expanding fluid, with a shear viscosity to entropy ratio $\eta/s$ close to that of a quantum fluid, is a viable description for the early stages of heavy-ion collisions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the radial flow velocity is a function of the initial eccentricity and the survival time of the initial perturbations.
a single value of shear viscosity to entropy ratio can explain the transverse momentum distributions and the flow harmonics at the LHC, for all the identified particles.
the transverse momentum dependence of elliptic flow and triangular flow can be used to extract the value of the $\eta/s$ ratio.
